shot_sizes.use: feet entering and stopping, legs on an arrival, a hand tightening on a strap, a back walking away; robust for image-to-video

camera_moves.intent: a turning point, two people bound together

camera_rules: One camera move per shot; never stack moves (no push-in plus pan plus tilt).
Name the move, its speed and the end framing; the move must be able to reach that framing.
Never write zoom for a physical move: push-in, pull-out, tracking, pan, tilt.
No three consecutive cuts sharing both shot size and camera move.

lenses.intent: tight emotional close-up, isolation from the background
natural perspective, mid dialogue and two-shots

lenses.use: object inserts with focus locked on the object

setups.intent: threat, a secret, a divided face
longing, separation, a silhouette at a door
night confession, loneliness (lamp, phone screen, convenience-store neon)

lighting.rule: One motivated source per scene, named once, same direction on every shot of that scene.

action_reaction.definition: The basic unit of coverage: an action (a line, a gesture, a piece of information) and the reaction it causes (a face, a silence, a change in the space).
action_reaction.routine_share: about 70% of units are routine (standard pair, stacked actions, escalation, chained); about 30% are memorable variants used at the beats that matter

variants.use: clear cause and effect; the backbone

variants.pattern: reaction, then the action that caused it
variants.use: a shocked face, then the message on the phone: curiosity window
pressure builds, the reaction carries all of it

variants.pattern: action, then cut away without the reaction
variants.use: the heaviest line of the episode; once or twice at most

variants.pattern: action heard off screen, picture on the reaction
variants.use: a slap, a door, a voice behind the character

variants.pattern: action, ordinary behaviour, then the reaction breaks
action and reaction in one frame
variants.use: speaker in front, listener behind, no cut
news lands on a family or an office

variants.pattern: B's reaction is the next action
variants.use: keeps a scene moving without a break

variants.pattern: same action with small changes, different reactions

cut_logic: Most cuts move one scale step (wide to medium, medium to close-up); about 40-47% of micro-drama cuts keep the same scale.
A two-step jump (wide straight to close-up) is a shock device for a reveal or a break.
Inside a scene the scale tends to move closer as the scene deepens; pull back to end it or to reveal.
Open a new scene with a wide, or with a detail insert that the next shots explain.
Change the angle only when the power balance changes.

dialogue_coverage.use: the listener's shoulder in the foreground, out of focus
shot/reverse that moves one scale closer as the conflict rises
both in frame, no cut: equality or intimacy
the line plays on the listener's face; weight lives in the reaction
both face the same way: closeness without confrontation, or avoidance
talking through a mirror or glass: a split or false self
through a door gap or window: someone overhears

dialogue_choice: Equal power: two-shot. Domination: scale or angle difference. Conflict: shot/reverse moving closer. Avoidance: profile or back. Intimacy: hold without cutting.

editing.rule: Cut in the middle of a movement; the next shot continues it from the same pose.
A look off screen is answered by what is seen (eyeline match), from roughly that point of view.
Keep the camera on one side of the line between two speakers; cross only with a visible move or a neutral shot.
A character exiting frame right enters the next shot from frame left.
Let the next shot's sound or line start over the end of the current shot to pull the viewer forward.
Let a line continue over the listener's reaction shot.
Hold only while a reaction is still developing; a hold with nothing changing is dead air.
End and start neighbouring shots on the same gesture so independently generated clips cut together.

acting: Give the eyes a task aimed at the partner (checking, avoiding, measuring, catching a lie); dead eyes are the main AI tell.
The reaction starts before the partner's line ends; a hard question earns a short pause before the answer.
Write an objective (make him confess), never a state (be angry).
Small and contained: the tighter the shot, the less movement; only the eyes and one change of expression on a close-up.
Give hands a task (business); the strongest accent is the moment it stops.
Distance is drama: closing or breaking distance is a beat.
The powerful stay still and quiet; the weak fidget. Everyone freezes at the threat.
States have inertia: no instant recovery after a strong event.
Group reactions arrive in a staggered wave, never in sync.

bad_acting.fix: drop the face from the task; give the objective and a hand task
mark 2-4 beats with a new tactic each
the gesture precedes, contradicts or is absent
build restraint before the break; emotion needs a trigger
on a close-up only the eyes and the thought
fill with assessment or a task, or cut

director_styles.look: handheld at arm's length, medium and medium close-up, natural grey-blue light, real practicals
director_styles.rhythm: long takes; the painful moment happens in one shot without a cut
director_styles.use: everyday grief and attrition; no music cue telling the viewer to cry

director_styles.look: precisely staged moves, vertical space (stairs, slopes) as class, frames split by windows and walls
director_styles.rhythm: the cut speed changes with the genre inside one scene
director_styles.use: social tension, a comedy that turns into a threat

director_styles.look: painterly symmetry for formality, tilted or obstructed frames for desire, curtains and frosted glass
director_styles.rhythm: long gazes, then a burst of fast cuts

durations.note: Shanyin short-film references (551 shots, 9 films): average 4.2 s, median 3 s; Higgsfield: one dialogue line 3-7 s, wordless reaction 5-10 s. Vertical micro-drama is about twice as fast: see dramaboard_rhythm.json.
